newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican peso could hit 8 per dollar soon - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Mexican peso could hit 8 per dollar soon - analysts.

text.p: Battered over the past week, Mexico's peso will likely fall further against the dollar in the next few weeks before recovering slightly towards the year end, economists said on Wednesday.

Although it had been one of the world's strongest currencies this year against the dollar, the peso has suddenly fallen victim to growing worries about its value and domestic seasonal factors such as inflation.

In the past week, the peso has fallen from about 7.52 per dollar to 7.80 per dollar -- a slide that has worried traders who still remember the turbulent months that followed its spectacular December 1994 crash.
On Wednesday, the peso was down 8 centavos at midday to 7.79/7.805 per dollar in its widely-watched 48-hour contracts.
Some Mexican economists were sanguine about the peso on Wednesday, saying they had expected the currency to begin adjusting toward year-end expectations of about 8.00 per dollar.

A survey of Mexican economists by Reuters MXAAP forecasts a year-end peso at 7.86 per dollar -- only slightly below current levels. Analysts had originally forecast a lower level for the peso, but many adjusted their predictions in recent weeks, thinking the peso might stay strong.
"This is a temporary thing...we had a similar situation during this time last year, but our fundamentals are much better right now," said a top economist at a top Mexican bank.

The economist expects the peso to test 8.00 per dollar in the coming weeks as investors buy dollars to protect themselves against any surprises in the government's economic plan for 1997, which is due to be unveiled before November 15.
The government plan will include public sector price rises for next year that could affect inflation expectations.
"We are in a turbulent area. Until the new government plan is announced, we cannot discount new shocks," said Enrique Quintana, a columnist for Mexico City daily Reforma.

Threat of interest rate or currency intervention by the Banco de Mexico will likely prevent an all-out speculative attack, however. Last year, the Banco de Mexico ended a run on the peso in November by selling dollars.

Economists said the peso's current weakness can be explained also by fundamentals. Interest rates in Mexico had fallen most of this year and were their lowest in both real and nominal terms since before the devaluation.
Declining trade surpluses during August and September, meanwhile, added weight to comments by U.S. economist Rudiger Dornbusch that the peso was in danger of becoming overvalued.

"This is a natural cycle for the peso under the current system...interest rates fall until some exogenous factor causes the peso to fall and rates to back up," said Ernesto O'Farrill, director of Mexico City consultant Bursametrica.
The government's move to scale back its privatization of the petrochemicals industry also had a psychological effect on investors -- giving some an excuse to sell pesos.

O'Farrill said the peso's ups and downs will likely continue until the Banco de Mexico can build enough reserves to credibly defend the currency. Net central bank assets remain below $4 billion, according to latest official figures.
"The central bank should have been more aggressive in building reserves this year. That would avoid these types of shocks," he said.
O'Farrill sees a year-end peso at 8.10 per dollar. He expects interest rates to rise again in the coming weeks as the central bank tries to defend the peso.
